title: We Know How to Worry About AI That Fails
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Richard Claydon introduces his five-part field-note series, AI Beyond the Business Case, by shifting attention from AI that fails to AI that works. His central illustration is a deliberately clean scenario: a global company whose Finance, Customer Success, Sales, Service, and Deal Desk agents all have valid data, stay within permissions, and hit their local objectives, yet collectively send one strategic customer a payment warning, a service credit, an expansion pitch, and an adoption intervention at once. The point is that the failure lives between components, where no local reviewer sees an error, and he coins 'shadow agency' for digital actors that shape outcomes while their combined behaviour remains only partially visible. Claydon then reflects on why executives shrug at the scenario, weighing three explanations: an abstract framing, AI metaphors of tsunamis that make consequences feel inevitable, and a pre-existing deficit in system-level leadership capacity. He settles on the third, arguing that agentic AI changes the tempo of cross-boundary sense-making, accountability, authority, and judgement without simplifying the leadership work, and that governance must extend from individual agents to the whole agent estate.
points: In Claydon's scenario, five correctly functioning agents each achieve their local goal and together produce an enterprise crisis, showing that there may be no defective component to find.
'Shadow agency' extends the shadow-IT problem: disconnected systems merely hold information, but disconnected agents can act on real business outcomes.
Governance needs to know not just that an agent exists but what it can see and change, what responds to its changes, how fast actions propagate, and who has authority to interrupt the pattern.
Describing AI as a wave or tsunami casts executives as survivors of an external force, quietly making unintended organisational consequences seem inevitable.
Claydon's preferred diagnosis is that AI exposes an existing leadership gap in seeing across functions, holding competing interpretations, and tracing second-order consequences, now at machine speed.
quotes: Every individual action makes sense from where that agent sits. Together, they produce something faintly ridiculous.

A human reviewer sitting inside Finance sees a valid debt action. A reviewer in Service sees a legitimate credit. Sales sees a genuine commercial signal. There may be no local error for any of them to reject.
I use the term shadow agency for one aspect of this condition: digital actors able to influence real business outcomes while their combined behaviour remains only partially visible to the enterprise.

Those metaphors convey scale and speed very effectively. They also create a particular kind of executive role. You prepare for a tsunami. You adapt to it. You survive the impact and deal with the aftershocks. Once we start thinking this way, unintended organisational consequences can quietly acquire the status of inevitability.

These problems demand the ability to see across functional boundaries, hold several legitimate interpretations at the same time, trace second-order consequences and create sufficient authority to intervene across a system. Many organisations already find that difficult when every actor involved is human.
Sense-making becomes more demanding when no single perspective contains the problem. Accountability becomes more complicated when several actors have done exactly what they were supposed to do.
And organisations are systems of authority, relationships, information, incentives, expertise, attention and competing interpretations. AI increasingly enters all of them at once.
What I find increasingly difficult to believe is that an enterprise full of correctly functioning digital actors will somehow organise itself.
